question: Under AS 08.88.165, a person who does not hold an Alaska real estate license may conduct an auction of real estate only if which condition is met?
choice_a: The auctioneer has completed an auctioneering program that included a real estate sales course, and a licensed broker or associate broker supervises and is present during the auction
choice_b: The auctioneer has passed the Alaska real estate salesperson examination within the preceding 12 months
choice_c: The property owner personally requests in writing that the auction be conducted by an unlicensed auctioneer
choice_d: The auction is limited to residential property valued under $250,000
explanation: AS 08.88.165 exempts a person from licensure for conducting a real estate auction only if the person completed a certified auctioneering program that included a real estate sales course AND a licensed broker or associate broker supervises and is present during the auction. Choice B invents an unrelated exam-recency rule; C and D are not conditions found in the statute.

question: Under AS 08.88.167, what is the maximum civil penalty the Alaska Real Estate Commission may levy against a person for engaging in unlicensed real estate activity, for a single offense?
choice_a: A flat $1,000 fine regardless of circumstances
choice_b: $5,000, or the amount of gain realized plus $5,000, whichever is greater
choice_c: Loss of the right to ever apply for an Alaska real estate license
choice_d: Twice the commission earned on the transaction, capped at $10,000
explanation: AS 08.88.167(b) caps the civil penalty at $5,000, or the gain realized plus $5,000, whichever is greater, for each offense, after the commission considers the seriousness of the violation, economic benefit, and history of violations. A, C, and D do not reflect the statutory formula.
source_note: AS 08.88.167(b) (Civil penalty for unlicensed or unauthorized practice)

question: AS 08.88.900(a)(2) exempts an attorney-in-fact acting under a power of attorney authorizing a specific real estate transaction from licensure. What limitation does the statute place on this exemption?
choice_a: The exemption applies only to transactions involving family members
choice_b: The attorney-in-fact must be a licensed attorney admitted to the Alaska Bar
choice_c: The attorney-in-fact may not act under this exemption for more than two transactions in a calendar year
choice_d: The exemption is available only for commercial, not residential, property
explanation: AS 08.88.900(a)(2) exempts an attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney authorizing a specific transaction, but caps use of this exemption at two transactions per calendar year. The statute does not require the person to be an admitted attorney (that is a separate exemption under (a)(3)), nor does it limit the exemption by family relationship or property type.

question: An employee of a domestic corporation manages and sells real estate owned by that corporation as part of the employee's regular duties, exempt from licensure under AS 08.88.900(a)(9). Under that provision, when does the employee LOSE the exemption?
choice_a: The exemption is never lost once granted
choice_b: If the corporation owns more than five parcels of real estate
choice_c: If the employee has never taken a real estate course
choice_d: If the employee performs the activity as a vocation, or receives compensation dependent on or directly related to the value of the real estate
explanation: AS 08.88.900(a)(9) exempts an employee of a corporation, partnership, or LLC who handles the employer's own real estate incidentally, but the exemption expressly does not apply if the person performs the activity as a vocation or is compensated in a way tied to the value of the real estate. B and C are not conditions found in the statute, and A is incorrect because the exemption can be lost.

question: Under AS 08.88.900(a)(16), a natural person may manage residential rental property for other owners without holding an Alaska real estate license, as long as the total number of units managed does not exceed:
choice_a: Four
choice_b: Ten
choice_c: One
choice_d: Twenty-five
explanation: AS 08.88.900(a)(16) exempts "the management of a total of four or fewer residential units by a natural person for other persons" from the license requirement. None of the other unit counts appear in the statute.

question: A property owner personally manages their own rental property under an exemption in AS 08.88.900. A licensed broker who referred a tenant to the owner wants to pay the owner a referral fee tied to the resulting lease. What does AS 08.88.900(b) say about this arrangement?
choice_a: The referral fee is permitted because the owner is exempt from licensing
choice_b: AS 08.88.401(d)(1) still prohibits the licensee from knowingly paying any part of a commission or fee to the exempt, unlicensed person
choice_c: The fee is permitted only if disclosed to the commission in writing within 10 days
choice_d: The fee is permitted up to $500 per referral
explanation: AS 08.88.900(b) clarifies that even though a person may be exempt from the licensing chapter for their own activity, AS 08.88.401(d)(1) still bars a licensee from knowingly paying a fee or commission to that unlicensed person for an act requiring a license. A, C, and D contradict this rule.

question: Under AS 08.88.900(a)(12), a secretary or receptionist in a real estate office may accept rent or community association fees from a tenant or association member without holding a real estate license, provided that:
choice_a: The secretary has at least one year of office experience
choice_b: The amount collected is under $1,000
choice_c: The secretary provides a written receipt for the rent or fees
choice_d: The broker is physically present at the time of collection
explanation: AS 08.88.900(a)(12) exempts a secretary or receptionist in a real estate office who accepts rent or association fees and provides a written receipt when a tenant or community association member delivers them. There is no experience threshold, dollar cap, or broker-presence requirement in the statute.

question: Under AS 08.88.251(a), what must a real estate licensee do to place their license on inactive status?
choice_a: Simply stop practicing and wait for the license to lapse automatically
choice_b: Notify only the employing broker; no filing with the commission is required
choice_c: Pay a $50 inactivation penalty and surrender all continuing education credits earned
choice_d: Return the license certificate and a completed inactivation form to the commission, along with any applicable fees
explanation: AS 08.88.251(a) requires the licensee to return the license certificate and a completed inactivation form to the commission along with any applicable fees; the commission then issues an inactive license certificate. B, C, and D (other than the correct choice) misstate this process.

question: Under AS 08.88.251(b), an inactive Alaska real estate licensee may not attempt or offer to perform any activity listed in AS 08.88.161, but the statute does permit the inactive licensee to:
choice_a: Receive commissions or other payments from the broker who previously contracted with or employed the licensee, for services performed while actively licensed
choice_b: Continue listing new properties as long as another active licensee co-signs the listing
choice_c: Supervise unlicensed assistants who are performing licensed activities
choice_d: Renew the inactive license indefinitely with no time limit
explanation: AS 08.88.251(b) allows an inactive licensee to receive commissions or payments earned for work performed while actively licensed, even though the person may not engage in new licensed activity while inactive. D is also wrong on its own terms, since 251(d) caps inactive-license renewal at 24 months from the anniversary date of the original inactive certificate.

question: A licensee has held an inactive Alaska real estate license for 30 months and now wants to become active again. Under AS 08.88.251(c), what must this person do?
choice_a: Simply file a reactivation form and pay a small fee, since less than three years have passed
choice_b: Meet the requirements applicable to initial licensure under this chapter, because the inactive period reached 24 months or more
choice_c: Retake only the state-specific portion of the exam
choice_d: Nothing extra is required; reactivation is automatic after any period of inactivity
explanation: AS 08.88.251(c) allows straightforward reactivation only if the licensee has been inactive for less than 24 months. Once inactive status reaches 24 months or more, the person must instead meet the qualifications for initial licensure under AS 08.88.171. A, C, and D misstate the rule.

question: A real estate license lapsed 20 months ago. Under AS 08.88.241, what must the person provide to be eligible for reinstatement rather than having to qualify as a brand-new applicant?
choice_a: Nothing; a lapsed license can never be reinstated
choice_b: Only proof that they have not been convicted of a crime
choice_c: A completed application, license fees, proof of continuing education for the lapsed periods, and proof of any applicable education requirements under AS 08.88.095(a)
choice_d: Proof that the license was inactive, not lapsed, for the entire period
explanation: AS 08.88.241(a) permits reinstatement of a license lapsed less than 24 months upon submission of the application, fees, proof of continuing education for the periods the license was inactive or lapsed, and proof of AS 08.88.095(a) education if applicable. A license lapsed 24 months or more instead requires meeting the initial-licensure qualifications under 241(b).

question: A licensed salesperson requests a license transfer from Broker A to Broker B. Under 12 AAC 64.075(b), what is Broker A's deadline for completing and submitting the broker notice of licensee termination form to the commission?
choice_a: Immediately, within 24 hours
choice_b: Within 30 days
choice_c: There is no deadline; it may be submitted at the broker's convenience
choice_d: Not later than five days from the date of the licensee's request for a license transfer
explanation: 12 AAC 64.075(b) requires the terminating broker to complete the termination form, give a copy to the licensee, and submit it to the commission not later than five days after the licensee's request for a license transfer. The other timeframes do not match the regulation.

question: Under 12 AAC 64.075(c), after applying for a license transfer, for how long may a licensee work in the new employing broker's office while waiting for the amended license certificate?
choice_a: Not more than 30 days
choice_b: Indefinitely, until the amended certificate is denied
choice_c: Not more than 7 days
choice_d: Only after the amended certificate has physically arrived
explanation: 12 AAC 64.075(c) permits the licensee to work in the new broker's office for not more than 30 days while the amended license certificate is pending, with the new broker required to keep copies of the transfer application and termination form until the certificate arrives.

question: Under 12 AAC 64.075(e), what happens if a licensee fails to notify the commission of a broker transfer or status change within 15 days after the commission receives notice from the terminating broker?
choice_a: The license is automatically revoked
choice_b: The licensee's period of active and continuous experience is interrupted
choice_c: The licensee is fined $500 per day of delay
choice_d: Nothing; the 15-day period is only a courtesy guideline with no consequence
explanation: 12 AAC 64.075(e) provides that a licensee's failure to notify the commission within 15 days interrupts the licensee's active and continuous experience, which matters because AS 08.88.171 requires 36 months of active, continuous experience within the preceding 60 months for broker eligibility. It does not automatically revoke the license or impose a per-day fine.

question: Under 12 AAC 64.080(b), what happens to the licenses of the associate brokers and salespersons employed by a broker whose license is suspended or revoked?
choice_a: Nothing changes; they may continue practicing under a temporary broker of record
choice_b: They are immediately upgraded to independent broker status
choice_c: Their licenses are automatically and simultaneously suspended
choice_d: They have 90 days to find a new broker before any action is taken against them
explanation: 12 AAC 64.080(b) provides that when a real estate broker's license is suspended or revoked, the licenses of every associate broker and salesperson employed by that broker are automatically and simultaneously suspended, with the commission notifying them after the order is served on the employing broker. A, B, and D are incorrect.
source_note: 12 AAC 64.080(b) (Suspension and revocation of active licenses)

question: Under AS 08.88.301, what must a real estate broker do before changing the location of the broker's principal office or a branch office?
choice_a: Nothing is required until the next license renewal cycle
choice_b: Obtain written consent from all licensees employed at that office
choice_c: Publish a public notice of the move in a local newspaper
choice_d: Notify the commission of the new address and any other office changes on the form provided by the commission, and pay the applicable fees
explanation: AS 08.88.301 requires the broker to notify the commission of the new address and any other office changes on the commission's form and pay applicable fees before moving the principal office or a branch office. B, C, and D (other than the correct choice) are not statutory requirements.

question: Under AS 08.88.398, a licensed real estate salesperson may act as a "licensed assistant" to another salesperson or associate broker only if several conditions are met. Which of the following is one of those conditions?
choice_a: The licensed assistant and the salesperson or associate broker being assisted must both be employed by the same broker
choice_b: The licensed assistant must hold a broker's license, not a salesperson's license
choice_c: The licensed assistant may work simultaneously for up to three different employing brokers
choice_d: The arrangement may be oral, as long as both parties agree
explanation: AS 08.88.398(1) requires that the licensed assistant and the salesperson or associate broker they assist be employed by the same broker. Contrary to choice B, the assistant may hold a salesperson or associate broker license; contrary to C, AS 08.88.398(2) bars performing licensed activities for more than one broker; contrary to D, AS 08.88.398(3) requires the arrangement to be in writing.

question: Under AS 08.88.398(5)-(6), who is responsible for the licensed assistant's wages/taxes and who agrees to be liable for the licensed assistant's actions?
choice_a: The Real Estate Commission handles both wages and liability
choice_b: The salesperson or associate broker who employs the assistant pays wages and taxes; the employing broker agrees to be liable for the assistant's actions
choice_c: The licensed assistant is solely responsible for their own wages, taxes, and liability
choice_d: Liability and wage responsibility are waived by statute once the assistant is licensed
explanation: AS 08.88.398(5) makes the salesperson or associate broker who employs the licensed assistant responsible for the assistant's wages and appropriate taxes, while 398(6) requires the broker of that salesperson or associate broker to agree to be liable for the licensed assistant's actions. A, C, and D misstate this division of responsibility.

question: Under 12 AAC 64.095(b), which of the following tasks may a real estate licensee ask an UNLICENSED person to perform?
choice_a: Show the property to a prospective buyer without the licensee present
choice_b: Explain the terms of a listing contract to the seller
choice_c: Unlock a listed property so it can be viewed by a licensee, remain during the showing, and relock it afterward
choice_d: Host an open house at the property
explanation: 12 AAC 64.095(b)(7) specifically permits an unlicensed person to unlock a property for a licensee's showing, remain during it, and relock it afterward. Showing property, explaining listing contract terms, and hosting an open house are all listed as prohibited activities for unlicensed persons under 12 AAC 64.095(a).
source_note: 12 AAC 64.095(a)-(b) (Real estate activities of unlicensed persons)

question: Under 12 AAC 64.095(b)(2), an unlicensed person employed by a real estate licensee may schedule appointments for the licensee, but this permission specifically does NOT extend to:
choice_a: Answering the office phone
choice_b: Placing signs on listed property
choice_c: Acting as a courier for documents
choice_d: Telephonic solicitation or soliciting business on behalf of the licensee
explanation: 12 AAC 64.095(b)(2) allows an unlicensed person to schedule appointments for the licensee, but expressly excludes telephonic solicitation or soliciting business on the licensee's behalf from that permission. Answering phones, placing signs, and acting as a courier are separately allowed under other subparagraphs of 12 AAC 64.095(b).
source_note: 12 AAC 64.095(b)(2) (Real estate activities of unlicensed persons)

question: Under 12 AAC 64.140(b), which of the following may a licensee NOT authorize an unlicensed assistant to do?
choice_a: Present an offer to a seller
choice_b: File office documents and order items needed for routine repair
choice_c: Compute commission checks
choice_d: Record and deposit trust funds, including transaction deposits and security deposits
explanation: 12 AAC 64.140(b)(5) specifically prohibits a licensee from authorizing an unlicensed assistant to present an offer to a seller, along with discussing listing terms, negotiating a sale, or having a buyer sign an offer. Filing documents, ordering repair supplies, computing commission checks, and recording/depositing trust funds are all listed as permitted clerical and bookkeeping tasks under 12 AAC 64.095(b).
source_note: 12 AAC 64.140(b); 12 AAC 64.095(b) (contrast of prohibited vs. permitted unlicensed tasks)

question: Under 12 AAC 64.140(a), retaining the services of a person as a real estate salesperson or associate broker who is not licensed under AS 08.88 is:
choice_a: Permitted if the person is a family member of the broker
choice_b: Grounds for revocation or suspension of the employing licensee's license
choice_c: Permitted for the first 90 days while a license application is pending
choice_d: Only a civil matter between the broker and the unlicensed person, not a licensing violation
explanation: 12 AAC 64.140(a)(1) lists retaining the services of an unlicensed person to act as a salesperson or associate broker as grounds for revocation or suspension of the employing licensee's license. No exception exists for family members or a grace period while an application is pending, and it is squarely a licensing violation, not merely a private civil matter.

question: Under AS 08.88.172(a), errors and omissions insurance in Alaska is:
choice_a: Optional, recommended only for brokers who manage trust accounts
choice_b: Required only for licensees who have previously been the subject of a complaint
choice_c: A condition of licensing that every real estate broker, associate broker, and salesperson must carry and maintain
choice_d: Provided automatically at no cost to all licensees by the Real Estate Commission
explanation: AS 08.88.172(a) makes errors and omissions insurance a mandatory condition of licensing for every real estate broker, associate broker, and salesperson, to cover activities requiring licensure under AS 08.88.161. It is not optional, complaint-triggered, or free.

question: Under 12 AAC 02.510(a)(1), the master errors and omissions insurance policy must provide each individual licensee a limit of liability of not less than:
choice_a: $50,000 per covered wrongful act or claim
choice_b: $250,000 per covered wrongful act or claim
choice_c: $1,000,000 per covered wrongful act or claim
choice_d: $100,000 per covered wrongful act or claim
explanation: 12 AAC 02.510(a)(1) sets the minimum per-wrongful-act (or per-claim) limit at $100,000, with claims expenses such as investigation and defense costs required to be in addition to that limit. The other dollar figures do not match the regulation.

question: Under 12 AAC 02.510(a)(2), the master errors and omissions insurance policy must provide each licensee an annual aggregate limit of liability of not less than:
explanation: 12 AAC 02.510(a)(2) requires a minimum annual aggregate limit of liability of $300,000 per licensee, which is distinct from the $100,000 minimum per-covered-wrongful-act/per-claim limit set in (a)(1). The other figures are not the regulatory minimum.

question: Under 12 AAC 02.510(a)(3), the deductible for each covered wrongful act under the master errors and omissions policy may not exceed what amount for every $300,000 of annual aggregate limit of liability?
explanation: 12 AAC 02.510(a)(3) caps the deductible for each covered wrongful act at $5,000 for every $300,000 of annual aggregate limit of liability, though an additional deductible for investigation and defense costs may also apply. The other amounts are not the regulatory cap.

question: Under 12 AAC 02.550, what is the maximum annual premium that may be charged a licensee under the master errors and omissions insurance policy?
explanation: 12 AAC 02.550 caps the maximum annual premium chargeable to a licensee under the master errors and omissions policy at $2,500. Coverage amounts, but not this premium cap, may be periodically adjusted by the department under 12 AAC 02.560.

question: Under 12 AAC 02.530(2), a broker who employs other real estate licensees may satisfy the individual per-claim and aggregate coverage requirements of 12 AAC 02.510(a)(1)-(2) by obtaining a policy covering all associated licensees with a minimum of:
choice_a: $100,000 per wrongful act and $300,000 aggregate
choice_b: $50,000 per wrongful act and $150,000 aggregate
choice_c: $1,000,000 per wrongful act with no aggregate limit
choice_d: $300,000 per wrongful act and $1,000,000 aggregate
explanation: 12 AAC 02.530(2) allows a broker who employs other licensees to satisfy the coverage standard through a single policy providing at least $300,000 per wrongful act and $1,000,000 aggregate, as long as all licensees associated with the broker are covered. Choice A restates the individual master-policy minimums rather than the broker blanket alternative; C and D (other than the correct choice) do not appear in the regulation.

question: Under 12 AAC 02.510(c)(1), the insurer selected to provide the master errors and omissions insurance policy must maintain what minimum A.M. Best rating and financial size category?
choice_a: "B+" rating and financial size category class VI or higher
choice_b: "A" rating and financial size category class X or higher
choice_c: "C" rating with no financial size requirement
choice_d: No specific rating is required as long as the insurer is licensed in Alaska
explanation: 12 AAC 02.510(c)(1) requires the master-policy insurer to maintain an A.M. Best rating of "B+" or better and a financial size category of class VI or higher, in addition to holding a certificate of authority under AS 21.09. B, C, and D misstate or omit this requirement.

question: Under 12 AAC 02.520(3), the master errors and omissions policy may exclude coverage for claims arising from a criminal, dishonest, fraudulent, or intentional act by the insured, EXCEPT for:
choice_a: Any insured who self-reports within 24 hours, regardless of whether they participated in the act
choice_b: An insured person who did not personally participate in the act and, upon learning of it, reported it to the Real Estate Commission or appropriate law enforcement authorities
choice_c: An insured whose act caused less than $10,000 in damages
choice_d: There is no exception; such acts are always excluded from coverage
explanation: 12 AAC 02.520(3) carves out an exception to the criminal/dishonest/fraudulent/intentional-act exclusion for an insured who did not personally participate in the wrongful act and, upon learning of it, reported it to the Real Estate Commission or the appropriate law enforcement authorities. A, C, and D misstate the exception.
